identity.title: Tex11 mutant mouse models of human azoospermia.

content.abstract: STUDY QUESTION: Do different patient TEX11 mutations lead to non-obstructive azoospermia (NOA) when modeled in mice? SUMMARY ANSWER: A frameshift mutation in Tex11 leads to azoospermia in mice (Tex11D); a missense mutation had no impact on fertility (Tex11A); and a splice site mutation caused reduced testis weights and sperm counts with variable sub-fertility (Tex11L). WHAT IS KNOWN ALREADY: Half of all NOA cases are unexplained but may arise from unidentified genetic mutations. Several variants in TEX11 have been identified in men with NOA; and Tex11 knockout in mice causes NOA. STUDY DESIGN, SIZE, DURATION: For fertility analysis of the different mutations, the sample sizes were as follows: n = 3 wild-type controls; n = 5 Tex11D; n = 3 Tex11A; and n = 3 Tex11L. Wild-type males and hemizygous mutant male mice in each Tex11 line were bred with two to four different wild-type females for fertility analysis. At 12 weeks, testes and epidiymides were then collected for histological analysis and sperm counts. Additional Tex11L mice (n = 3) and wild-type controls (n = 3) were bred for 52 weeks with 2 new wild-type females every 2-3 weeks, then testes and epididymides were collected for further analysis. Testes and epididymides from Tex11L mice (n = 3 for wild type and mutants) were also collected at 24 and 36 weeks of age for histological analyses. PARTICIPANTS/MATERIALS, SETTING, METHODS: TEX11 variants identified in male patients with NOA were introduced into the orthologous region of the mouse genome using CRISPR/Cas9 gene editing. Lines were expanded onto a DBA/2 background by breeding female heterozygous carriers to wild-type DBA/2 males. Hemizygous males from the third generation and beyond were used for fertility studies, gross tissue morphology, sperm counts, and histological analysis. MAIN RESULTS AND THE ROLE OF CHANCE: Compared to wild-type mice (145.0 +/- 17.56 mg testis weight; 1.72 +/- 0.50 million sperm/cauda epididymis; 6.42 +/- 0.73 pups/breeding), Tex11D mice had reduced testis weight (28.33 +/- 0.68 mg), no sperm in the epididymis, and were infertile with a maturation arrest testicular phenotype. We did not observe any spermatogenesis or fertility defects in Tex11A mice (145.0 mg +/- 0 mg; 1.52 +/- 0.11 million sperm/cauda; 5.83 +/- 0.81 pups/breeding) compared to wild type. Tex11L mice had reduced testis weight (78.33 +/- 16.41 mg) and reduced epididymal sperm counts (0.33 +/- 0.13 million/cauda epididymis) but a variable fertility phenotype (5.42 +/- 1.13 pups/breeding), with 2 out of 6 mice being subfertile. Tex11L mice also had variable testicular and epididymal defects, classified as mild or severe. LARGE SCALE DATA: Not applicable for this study. LIMITATIONS, REASONS FOR CAUTION: The sample sizes were limited for each mouse line. WIDER IMPLICATIONS OF THE FINDINGS: Our study shows the importance of validating NOA-associated variants in a mouse model. Our data suggest that different TEX11 variants produce a variety of phenotypes which could impact genetic counselling of patients with NOA. FUNDING: This study was supported by the Eunice Kennedy Shriver National Institute for Child Health and Human Development (NICHD) grant HD096723 to A.N.Y. and K.E.O. G.R.A. was supported by NICHD grant HD114406. DISCLOSURES: K.E.O. was an advisor to Paterna Biosciences. The authors declare that the research was conducted in the absence of any commercial or financial relationships that could be construed as a potential conflict of interest.
